why: The amount is the one field nothing downstream can do without. The strict parser refuses the message, the light-model fallback gets one attempt, and whatever it cannot read is quarantined -- never passed on as a zero.

MT103 writes 5810,46 with a comma. A parser that strips the separator instead of reading it reports 581,046.00 -- a hundredfold error inside a filing. This is the regression fixture for that specific bug.
With no :20: there is no key, so the quarantine record has to be findable by its position in the batch instead. A message that cannot be named is still a message that was lost.
Latin-1 bytes are not valid UTF-8. Reading the file must fail as a clean batch-level error or decode with replacement -- never a UnicodeDecodeError escaping to the caller.
A transfer cut short by a failed copy. The messages before the cut are real and must survive; the fragment must not be completed by guesswork.
31 June. A date parser that rolls over to 1 July silently moves the transaction into another month's batch -- and every detector is a time window.
A credit transfer cannot be negative. Accepting it would let a detector compute an aggregate that offsets real transfers against a sign error.
LLD §6's one loud failure. A file with nothing in it must be a client error before a run id is minted, not a clean report for an empty month.
The degenerate case of the same rule, and the one a retry loop is most likely to send.

Two messages, one reference. Both are read -- neither is corrupt -- but a report's flagged_transactions is a set of references, so a detector must not be able to count one transaction twice by seeing the same ref in two places.
